Explanation: The selectable unit is a flight, stay or rental-car booking. Hopper can attach separately priced flexibility products such as Cancel for Any Reason or Disruption Assistance to that underlying travel transaction.

This case models Hopper together with its B2B division HTS. Hopper still operates a consumer travel app, but HTS is now the core commercial layer that distributes Hopper travel, fintech and commerce capabilities through outside brands.
Hopper has to combine travel supply, prediction, booking, servicing and optional flexibility into products that work in its own app and in partner channels.
Travel bookings create transaction economics, while dynamically priced flexibility products add high-margin ancillary revenue that can also be sold through external channels.

Hopper must price complex travel and flexibility products accurately, explain fees and limits clearly, manage claims and refunds, and maintain trust across both its own interface and partner channels.
Hopper matches demand with travel inventory, processes or enables the booking, and can attach paid flexibility products around cancellation, disruption or price uncertainty.
Transaction Flows: ← Consumer · Search / Buy — Travelers submit trip intent, choose inventory and complete a booking directly with Hopper or through an HTS-powered flow. | → Consumer · Booking / Flex — Hopper returns the booked travel product and can add separately priced flexibility such as cancellation or disruption assistance. | ← Provider · Inventory / Rates — Airlines, hotels and rental-car suppliers provide availability, prices and booking terms to the Hopper platform. | → Provider · Bookings / Pay — Confirmed demand and the applicable settlement or booking instructions flow back to the supplier that fulfills the trip. | ← Partner · Channel / Demand — Banks, airlines and other partner brands contribute their customer channel, booking context and demand to HTS integrations. | → Partner · Fintech / Commerce — HTS supplies embedded travel-commerce technology and fintech ancillaries that the partner can sell inside its own interface.

Explanation: Hopper sets product eligibility, dynamic prices, refund and service rules, and disclosure requirements. A 2026 FTC order reinforced obligations around total-price disclosure, optional-fee consent and accurate product claims.
Hopper reaches travelers through its own app and web presence, while HTS embeds the same travel and fintech capabilities inside banks, airlines, hotels and other partner brands.
Core activities include fare and risk prediction, dynamic pricing, merchandising, booking, payments, fraud controls, customer servicing and partner integration.
Hopper relies on large-scale travel price data, demand signals, machine-learning models, travel-supply connectivity, payments and servicing infrastructure.
Consumers are travelers using the Hopper app or an HTS-powered partner channel to search, book and optionally add flexibility to flights, stays or rental cars.
Travelers want a good fare or room and confidence that price changes, cancellations or disruptions will not make the trip unexpectedly expensive or difficult to fix.
Price prediction can improve booking timing, while paid flexibility products can provide cancellation or rebooking options beyond the base fare or room policy.
Travel prices move, many fares are restrictive, and delays or cancellations can create costly changes after the traveler has committed.
Travelers search and select travel inventory, complete a booking and may add a paid flexibility product during checkout.
Transaction Flows: → Owner · Search / Buy — Travelers submit trip intent, choose inventory and complete a booking directly with Hopper or through an HTS-powered flow. | ← Owner · Booking / Flex — Hopper returns the booked travel product and can add separately priced flexibility such as cancellation or disruption assistance.

Explanation: Travelers narrow by route or destination, dates, price and travel attributes, then decide whether extra flexibility is worth its price for that booking.
Consumers can use Hopper directly or encounter Hopper/HTS capabilities inside the websites and apps of partner banks, airlines and travel brands.
They search, compare, book, monitor prices and decide whether to purchase cancellation or disruption protection around the trip.
Travelers contribute itinerary details, preferences, payment information, loyalty context and demand signals.

Providers are airlines, hotels, property operators and rental-car companies that supply the underlying seat, room, home or vehicle. They remain responsible for the core travel inventory even when Hopper adds fintech around it.
Travel suppliers want to sell unused seats, rooms and vehicles while maintaining control over their schedules, base prices and fulfillment rules.
Hopper and HTS can bring incremental demand and merchandising capabilities that help suppliers sell inventory and improve economics around each booking.
Suppliers must keep inventory and prices synchronized across channels, pay distribution economics and manage changes, cancellations and service obligations.
Suppliers provide live inventory, fares or room rates and receive confirmed bookings or settlement through the relevant Hopper or partner-channel flow.
Transaction Flows: → Owner · Inventory / Rates — Airlines, hotels and rental-car suppliers provide availability, prices and booking terms to the Hopper platform. | ← Owner · Bookings / Pay — Confirmed demand and the applicable settlement or booking instructions flow back to the supplier that fulfills the trip.

Explanation: Inventory must meet integration, availability, pricing and booking requirements, while individual fare or room terms still determine the underlying travel product.
Airlines and other suppliers connect through direct APIs, NDC, aggregators, hotel connectivity and other supply integrations.
Suppliers set inventory and base terms, accept bookings, operate the flight, stay or rental and handle supplier-side fulfillment responsibilities.
They contribute the physical travel capacity, availability, schedules, rates, policies and fulfillment capability that make the booking possible.

Partners are banks, airlines, hotels and other brands that embed HTS travel or fintech into their own customer channels. The same airline can be a Provider of a flight and a Partner when its direct checkout distributes an HTS flexibility product.
Partner brands want to keep travel and flexibility inside their own customer relationship instead of sending users to a separate OTA.
Embedding HTS can add travel utility, ancillary margin and loyalty value without the partner building the full travel-fintech stack itself.
Running travel commerce internally requires supply connections, payments, fraud controls, servicing, product pricing and operational support that many brands do not want to build alone.
Partners integrate HTS modules into their own channels, contribute customer access and booking context, and sell travel or fintech to their audience.
Transaction Flows: → Owner · Channel / Demand — Banks, airlines and other partner brands contribute their customer channel, booking context and demand to HTS integrations. | ← Owner · Fintech / Commerce — HTS supplies embedded travel-commerce technology and fintech ancillaries that the partner can sell inside its own interface.

Explanation: HTS products are selected and configured according to partner geography, channel, travel category, customer proposition and technical integration requirements.
HTS distributes capabilities through APIs, SDKs and embedded e-commerce integrations, including partner-controlled booking flows.
Partners surface the offer in their own interface, market it to customers and coordinate with HTS on booking, support and product operations.
Partners contribute existing customer relationships, trusted interfaces, loyalty programs, payment context and distribution reach.
